function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: The unit of measurement for the command execution time, such as 'seconds' or 'milliseconds'

message.reasoning: The user wants to set a timer for 10 seconds using the timeout command. They say "You should use timeout 10." So they want to run a command that waits 10 seconds. On Windows, the timeout command is used like "timeout /t 10". But they said "timeout 10". That might be a Linux command? Actually, "timeout" is a Linux command that runs a command with a time limit. But "timeout 10" alone would just wait 10 seconds? In Linux, "sleep 10" would wait. But "timeout 10" is not typical. However, maybe they want to run "timeout 10" which will wait 10 seconds and then exit. But "timeout" expects a command to run. But if you just run "timeout 10" it will wait 10 seconds and then exit. Actually, "timeout" in Linux is part of coreutils: "timeout DURATION COMMAND [ARG]..." So you need a command. But "timeout 10" alone will error. But maybe they want to run "timeout 10" as a command that just waits 10 seconds. But we can just run "timeout 10" and it will exit after 10 seconds. But we need to use the function to execute a system command. We can call the function with command "timeout 10" and unit "seconds". Let's do that.
